summary: Describes cases where bridging multiple links into a single subnet requires network-layer support, and specifies the IP-layer support that enables bridging in those cases using Neighbor Discovery proxies. It is an experimental protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: An Internet Protocol version 6 (IPv6) Neighbor Discovery proxy can connect segments that cannot use ordinary bridging. It forwards traffic and changes link-layer addresses in Neighbor Discovery messages so each segment can reach the proxy.

subtitle: IPv6 Neighbor Discovery proxying for joining segments when link-layer bridging cannot work.

tldr.problem: Some links cannot use ordinary link-layer bridging, but devices may still need to share one IPv6 subnet prefix.
tldr.mechanism: An ND proxy forwards packets between interfaces and substitutes its own link-layer address in messages that carry such addresses.
tldr.outcome: The RFC defines an Experimental approach and a Router Advertisement Proxy bit to help prevent loops; it adds no proxy authorization mechanism.

today: RFC 4389 is an Experimental RFC, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. The RFC itself does not add security mechanisms for authorizing Neighbor Discovery proxies.

sections.title: When Link-Layer Bridging Is Not Possible
sections.content:
Bridging several links into one subnet can simplify address management. Classic bridging requires promiscuous mode and compatible link-layer addressing, which some wireless client links and PPP links cannot provide.

RFC 4389 describes IPv6 network-layer support for these cases. It is intended for situations where classic bridging is not possible and router configuration is unavailable; the RFC says it does not apply to topologies with loops or routers on multiple segments.
sections.plainLanguage: Some links cannot pass all traffic the way a classic bridge requires. This experimental method lets IPv6 Neighbor Discovery help connect those segments.

sections.title: Design Goals and Limits
sections.content:
The proxy is designed to connect multiple segments under one subnet prefix without changing existing routers. It should provide connectivity among subnet nodes, prevent loops, support node movement, and allow a proxy to be added dynamically.

The RFC does not require shortest-path forwarding, a traceroute hop, or simultaneous use of every interface. It also does not cover non-IPv6 network-layer protocols or media where Neighbor Discovery cannot operate.
sections.plainLanguage: The proxy aims to connect subnet nodes without changes to existing routers. It has limits, including topologies with loops and media that cannot use Neighbor Discovery.

sections.title: Forwarding and Address Substitution
sections.content:
The proxy keeps a neighbor cache for each proxy interface. It forwards multicast traffic to the other interfaces and sends unicast traffic toward the interface with the best neighbor-cache entry. A packet is not sent back through the interface on which it arrived.

When forwarding, the proxy uses the outgoing interface's link-layer address as the source address and substitutes that address in packet payloads when those addresses may be used in later link-layer headers. If the outgoing interface has a smaller MTU than the packet, the proxy drops it and sends a Packet Too Big message.
sections.plainLanguage: The proxy uses its neighbor caches to choose an outgoing interface. It replaces link-layer addresses with its own address on that segment.

sections.title: Neighbor Discovery and Loop Prevention
sections.content:
The RFC gives special handling to Neighbor Solicitations, Neighbor Advertisements, Router Advertisements, and Redirects. A solicitation is forwarded rather than answered from the proxy's cache, so the proxy does not interfere with nodes moving between segments.

The RFC adds a Proxy bit, P, to Router Advertisements. An advertisement received upstream is forwarded downstream with this bit set. Interfaces that recently received certain advertisements cannot be used for proxying, and the proxy must send two P-bit advertisements downstream before enabling forwarding there.
sections.plainLanguage: The proxy forwards Neighbor Discovery messages while updating address information for each segment. The Proxy bit helps devices detect proxying and prevents loops.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Proxies have security weaknesses similar to hosts using unsecured Neighbor Discovery, including traffic hijacking and denial of service. A proxy also acts as a man-in-the-middle by design, so devices need a way to distinguish an authorized proxy from an attacker.

The RFC does not define a method to authorize proxies or extensions that let Secure Neighbor Discovery and proxies work together. Changes made by a proxy can invalidate a signature in a secured Neighbor Discovery message.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy changes Neighbor Discovery messages, and an attacker could imitate a proxy. This RFC does not define a way to authorize proxy devices.
